mpm.title: Managing Public Money
mpm.scope: In broad terms it applies to UK central government bodies, as well as other specified public sector bodies. The devolved administrations have equivalent rulebooks.

govs.title: Government Functional Standards (GovS 001 to GovS 015)
govs.scope: These standards are mandated for use across central government, and may also be adopted by other public sector organisations.

board-code.title: Code of Conduct for Board Members of Public Bodies
board-code.scope: Standards expected from those on boards of government departments, non-ministerial departments, executive agencies, NDPBs, and national public corporations.

cs-code.title: Civil Service Code
cs-code.scope: The Civil Service code outlines the Civil Service's core values, and the standards of behaviour expected of all civil servants.

lg-transparency.title: Local Government Transparency Code 2015
lg-transparency.scope: Sets out the minimum data that local authorities should be publishing, the frequency it should be published and how it should be published.

spfm.title: Scottish Public Finance Manual
spfm.scope: Issued by the Scottish Ministers, it sets out the main principles for dealing with resources in public sector organisations in Scotland; bodies sponsored by the Scottish Government include executive NDPBs, public corporations and NHS bodies.

mwpm.title: Managing Welsh Public Money
mwpm.scope: The framework applies to the Welsh Government, its sponsored bodies, the NHS in Wales, its commissioners, the Education Workforce Council, Estyn and the Welsh Government's subsidiary bodies.

mpmni.title: Managing Public Money Northern Ireland
mpmni.scope: It sets out the main principles for dealing with resources used by public sector organisations in Northern Ireland.

procurement-act.title: Procurement Act 2023
procurement-act.scope: A contracting authority is a public authority (or, for utilities contracts, also a public undertaking or private utility) other than an excluded authority; devolved Scottish authorities are excluded (section 2).

foi-depts.title: Freedom of Information Act 2000 (government departments)
foi-depts.scope: Schedule 1, Part I, paragraph 1: any government department, with named exceptions.

foi-lg.title: Freedom of Information Act 2000 (local government)
foi-lg.scope: Schedule 1, Part II: local authorities in England and Wales within the meaning of the Local Government Act 1972, and district councils in Northern Ireland.

foi-nhs.title: Freedom of Information Act 2000 (the NHS)
foi-nhs.scope: Schedule 1, Part III: bodies of the National Health Service.

psed.title: Equality Act 2010, public sector equality duty (section 149)
psed.scope: Schedule 19, Part 1 lists the authorities: a Minister of the Crown and government departments; a county, district or parish council in England; NHS bodies in England.

companies-act.title: Companies Act 2006
companies-act.scope: Applies to companies registered under it; the body has a Companies House number.

charities-act.title: Charities Act 2011
charities-act.scope: Applies to charities in England and Wales; the body has a Charity Commission registration number.

foisa-ministers.title: Freedom of Information (Scotland) Act 2002 (the Scottish Ministers)
foisa-ministers.scope: Schedule 1, Part 1, paragraph 1: the Scottish Ministers.

foisa-councils.title: Freedom of Information (Scotland) Act 2002 (local government)
foisa-councils.scope: Schedule 1, Part 3, paragraph 21: a council constituted by section 2 of the Local Government etc. (Scotland) Act 1994.

foisa-nhs.title: Freedom of Information (Scotland) Act 2002 (the NHS in Scotland)
foisa-nhs.scope: Schedule 1, Part 4 (The National Health Service): Health Boards, the Common Services Agency, Healthcare Improvement Scotland, the National Waiting Times Centre Board, NHS 24, Public Health Scotland, the Scottish Ambulance Service Board and others.

public-appointments.title: Governance Code on Public Appointments
public-appointments.scope: Applies to all public appointments made to bodies listed in the Public Appointments Order in Council; this body is on the list GOV.UK publishes (May 2026), matched by exact name.

government-organisation:PB295: S2 name plus a short form in brackets
nhs-ods:T1530: S2 name plus a short form in brackets

govt: Making laws, collecting taxes, keeping records, statistics and elections, and links with other countries.
defence: The armed forces and keeping the country safe from attack.
safety: Police, fire and rescue, courts, prisons and the justice system.
economy: Jobs, business, trade, farming, energy, roads, railways, ports and airports.
environment: Protecting nature, cleaning up pollution and looking after the countryside and sea.
housing: Housing, planning new buildings, water supply and improving towns and cities.
health: Hospitals, doctors, medicines and keeping people healthy.
culture: Museums, libraries, the arts, sport, broadcasting, languages and historic places.
education: Schools, colleges, universities, exams, skills and research.
support: Pensions, benefits, social care and support for children, families and disabled people.
local: Councils run many local services at once: bins, roads, schools, care, libraries and planning.
unknown: The sources don't say enough yet. You can help by sending a correction.

legislate: A parliament, assembly or council whose members debate and pass laws, approve spending and question the government.
policy: Ministers and civil servants who make policy, propose laws and run the departments under them.
judge: Courts and tribunals that settle disputes and decide what the law means in a case.
regulate: Licenses, registers or regulates a profession, market or activity, and can take action when rules are broken.
inspect: Checks that services and public money are run properly, and reports what it finds.
complaints: An ombudsman or commissioner who looks into complaints and stands up for people.
advise: A committee or council of experts that advises ministers but doesn't run services.
fund: Pays out grants, loans or investment to other organisations or people.
trade: Earns most of its income by charging customers, like a business.
collections: Museums, galleries, libraries, archives, parks and historic places.
records: Registers, records, maps and official statistics.
research: Science and research, in its own labs or by funding others.
promote: Promotes a place, an industry or a group of people, or speaks for them.
services: Delivers services to the public directly: health, councils, benefits, policing, transport and more.
unknown: The sources don't say enough yet. You can help by sending a correction.

legislature: Where elected (or appointed) members make laws, approve spending and question the government.
department: A ministerial or non-ministerial department, or a devolved government.
agency: Executive agency or part of a department
Run by civil servants inside a department, with its own job to do.
ndpb: Set up by law or by ministers to work at arm's length: an executive or advisory non-departmental public body, or another statutory body.
court: Where judges and tribunal members decide cases.
corporation: Owned or controlled by government and run like a business (ONS: public corporation).
nhs: A hospital trust, health board, care board or other NHS organisation.
council: An elected council, a group of councils, or a body that councils control.
central: A body ONS counts as central government that doesn't fit the groups above.
charity: A non-profit body that government partly funds or controls.
pension: A pension scheme for people who worked in public services.
territory: An overseas territory or Crown dependency with its own government.

local: Works in one council area or a few.
one: Works across one of England, Scotland, Wales or Northern Ireland.
several: Works in two or three of the four nations.
outside: A territory or Crown Dependency, or one of its bodies.
unstated: The sources don't say where it works yet.

type: Executive agency or part of a department

timeline.what: Ministers ask 63 councils about postponing their May 2026 elections; first mayoral elections in four priority areas moved to May 2028
The English Devolution and Community Empowerment Act becomes law
Council elections: 107 go ahead and 29 are postponed; East Surrey and West Surrey councils elected
Government sets out commencement: the supplementary vote returns for mayors and police and crime commissioners
Reorganisation review launched; decisions for Essex, Hampshire, Norfolk and Suffolk withdrawn
Five areas get 'minded to' decisions; July decisions for nine areas withdrawn; 15 areas under review
East Surrey and West Surrey councils take over
Elections to existing councils in the other 20 areas; first mayors elected in Cumbria and in Cheshire and Warrington
Elections to the new (shadow) councils; first mayors in Sussex and Brighton, Hampshire and the Solent, Greater Essex, and Norfolk and Suffolk
New single councils take over in the 20 remaining areas, if confirmed

meta.about: Local government in England under the English Devolution and Community Empowerment Act 2026: what is in force, and what is planned. Transcribed by hand from the primary sources linked on each fact, read on 22 November 2026. Secondary sources are used only where marked secondary, and only for a summary of the Act. Nothing here is inferred: a status the sources don't give is left out.

tiers.label: Single foundation strategic authority
tiers.plain: One county council or unitary council given strategic powers on its own.
tiers.law: A unitary district council or county council designated under section 3.

tiers.label: Combined foundation strategic authority
tiers.plain: Several councils working together as a combined authority, without a mayor.
tiers.law: A non-mayoral combined authority or combined county authority.

tiers.label: Mayoral strategic authority
tiers.plain: A group of councils with an elected mayor, who has more powers and money.
tiers.law: A mayoral combined authority, a mayoral combined county authority, or the Greater London Authority.

tiers.label: Established mayoral strategic authority
tiers.plain: A mayoral authority with a strong track record, given the most powers and a single funding settlement.
tiers.law: A mayoral strategic authority that has been designated as established.

value: Health, well-being and public service reform

changes.now: Mayors and police and crime commissioners are elected by the supplementary vote again: voters mark a first and a second choice. The May 2026 mayoral elections still used first past the post.
A mayor of a strategic authority can't also be a member of a UK legislature.
Councils can no longer choose the committee system of running a council. Most councils already use a leader and cabinet; a council with a 'protected' committee system may keep it but must review it.

summary.value: England's two-tier areas (a county council with district councils under it) are being replaced by single-tier unitary councils. There are 21 areas. Surrey's two new councils start on 1 April 2027. Five areas have 'minded to' decisions (29 October 2026). The other 15 are under review after decisions were withdrawn in September and October 2026; every area is due an outcome by early 2027.

Members: every open body that is a trading fund (trading fund orders on legislation.gov.uk and the ONS guide's notes)
or that ONS classifies as a public corporation (non-financial, financial, or the central bank).

trading-fund: A government operation that pays its way from what it charges, under the Government Trading Funds Act 1973. It still answers to a minister.
non-financial: Owned or controlled by government and sells goods or services, like a business (ONS: public non-financial corporation).
financial: Owned or controlled by government and lends, invests, insures or handles money (ONS: public financial corporation).
central-bank: The Bank of England and the bodies ONS counts with it.
